Thursday 19 November 2026, retrieved at 07:01 IST. Nvidia reports record revenue of 115.8 billion dollars, up 103 percent, and forecasts 130 billion dollars for the next quarter. The board has ruled out a return for Jensen Huang, and director Suzanne Norah Johnson will chair a new committee on national security and export controls while Colette Kress continues as interim chief executive. Isomorphic Labs has raised 5 billion dollars to move AI drug programs toward human trials. Gartner forecasts India's IT spending at 16.94 lakh crore rupees, a 10.6 percent increase, and also puts the figure near 17 lakh crore rupees by 2027.
The morning's through-line: Nvidia reports record revenue of 115.8 billion dollars with a 130 billion dollar forecast and has ruled out Jensen Huang's return, Isomorphic Labs has raised 5 billion dollars for AI drugs, and Gartner puts India's IT spending near 17 lakh crore rupees in 2027.
Nvidia's revenue. Nvidia reports record revenue of 115.8 billion dollars, up 103 percent, and forecasts 130 billion dollars for the next quarter. The same account looks at 32 billion dollars in agreements spelled Neoccloud. It says the board has ruled out a return for Jensen Huang.
The committee. Nvidia has formed a board committee to manage national security and global trade risks, including export controls, after shareholder lawsuits and an independent investigation. Director Suzanne Norah Johnson will chair it. Interim chief executive Colette Kress continues to manage daily operations. The move is described as a response to the regulatory environment around semiconductor trade. No new export rule is named.
Isomorphic Labs. Isomorphic Labs has secured 5 billion dollars to accelerate AI drug discovery and prepare candidates for human trials. Demis Hassabis is leading the company as internal programs move toward clinical testing. Sequoia Capital and Alphabet are named among the investors, not as a complete list. The research areas named are cancer and immunology. Preclinical results are described as a clear signal for AI-designed medicine. What those results showed is not stated.
India's IT bill. Gartner forecasts India's IT spending at 16.94 lakh crore rupees, a 10.6 percent increase, and also describes the outlook as 17 lakh crore rupees by 2027. The 16.94 lakh crore figure is also placed within the next few years. AI is described as a primary catalyst, influencing procurement and longer roadmaps. Demand is accelerating for data center systems and cloud infrastructure. A separate briefing says IT spending could approach 17 lakh crore rupees in 2027, with cloud infrastructure and data centres growing as technology budgets expand. That briefing does not repeat the 10.6 percent or the 16.94 lakh crore figure.
Karnataka. Karnataka has proposed a 200 mm semiconductor research and development fabrication facility at IISc as part of a semiconductor hub. A related facility is aimed at moving research toward manufacturing in advanced packaging, sensors, photonics, and quantum technologies. Another initiative targets support for 35 growth-stage deep tech ventures over five years. The state's AI hub is given as IIT Bangalore and is described as the first step toward a proposed AI university. Separately, Karnataka has announced six initiatives at the Bengaluru Tech Summit to scale AI, robotics, and semiconductor research, with investment in healthcare technology and advanced manufacturing. A robotics zone and a 200 mm chip fab are part of how that announcement is presented. The six initiatives are not named, and that announcement does not place the fab at IISc.
Electronics exports. Government figures put India's non-smartphone electronics exports at 13.79 billion dollars, up 56.5 percent, lifting their share of electronics exports to about 43 percent. The growth includes circuit boards, networking equipment, and memory products. Routing and network transmission equipment exports nearly doubled to 1.45 billion dollars. Mounted printed circuit boards reached 2.1 billion dollars, with Singapore accounting for most of those shipments. A broader reading puts electronics exports up 44 percent to 32 billion dollars in six months, from April to September, with smartphone manufacturing still dominant and non-smartphone electronics expanding quickly. That broader reading does not repeat the 13.79 billion dollar figure or the Singapore share.
The classrooms. Accenture and Google Cloud are launching AI training for students across India. Accenture LearnVantage is leading practical training for more than a thousand public and private schools and colleges. Students must pass assessments to earn certification in artificial intelligence. The programs cover core technical competencies, cloud skills, and AI implementation, and are meant to standardise tech education and scale digital literacy. A later account says the planned training will include generative AI and AI agents, and that a student who receives working code from an assistant still has to explain it, test it, and find the mistakes. That later account does not repeat the count of institutions or the LearnVantage name.
The summit. Day 2 of the Bengaluru Tech Summit is the 29th edition of what is described as Asia's largest integrated technology summit, running 17 to 19 November at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre under the theme AI and Beyond. The announced guests are D.K. Shivakumar, chief minister of Karnataka; Priyank Kharge, minister for home, information technology, biotechnology and e-governance; Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, executive chairperson of Biocon and chairperson of the state's Vision Group on Biotechnology; Pratik Gandhi, actor, storyteller and theatre practitioner; and Puneet Chandok, president of Microsoft India and South Asia. No remarks from them are established. Sanjana Gupta is reporting from the ground. The day is described as moving past inauguration speeches into enterprise AI, quantum computing, and space tech. The coverage takes in the Global Innovation Alliance and pavilions that include leading Chinese robotics firms, the difficulty Indian space startups face getting drop-test permissions from the defence sector, and a Karnataka push to place new global capability centres in tier-2 and tier-3 cities rather than Bengaluru. It also takes in reaction to 25 lakh rupees in state funding for startups and to Bengaluru's described status as the second most native-AI-ready city in Asia. Whether enterprise AI and deep tech are solving business problems beyond demonstrations is left open.
Cybersecurity. A Barracuda survey says AI is changing India's security teams, with an 81 percent AI skills gap and 66 percent of firms cutting headcount. Antara Gupta speaks with Rohit Aradhya, vice president of engineering and managing director at Barracuda, about that skills-versus-headcount paradox. The subjects are an AI-powered security operations centre, AI-generated phishing and business email compromise, zero trust against deepfakes and bypassed multi-factor authentication, where humans take over during an incident, missing skills, the changing role of the chief information security officer, the cost of AI security, and why accountability stays with people. What Aradhya concluded is not established.
Space recovery. Inbound Aerospace is building autonomous parachute systems to land reusable spacecraft, with a 2028 suborbital launch in sight. Sanjana Gupta speaks with co-founder Abhijit Bhutey at the Bengaluru Tech Summit. The conversation covers precision drop tests, steering a parachute autonomously, defence use and a provisional iDEX win, airspace and regulatory hurdles in India, re-entry rules and the Space Act, recovery in Australia and its cost, the next funding round, a path from the Indian Navy to the startup, and a step from Mach 2 to Mach 25. What Bhutey concluded is not established.
AI doctors. Point Break asks whether AI doctors can fill the gap left by missing hospitals, beds, and specialists. Antara Gupta speaks with Sidharth Srinivasan, chief executive of Lupin Digital Health; Dr. Sanjay Nagral, director of surgical gastroenterology at Jaslok Hospital; and Sudipta Sengupta, founder and chief executive of The Healthy Indian Project. The subjects are diagnosis, rural care, access and affordability, patient trust in chatbots, polypharmacy, continuity of care, the Ekacare and National Health Authority voice scribe, consent and data privacy, accountability when AI triage misses a diagnosis, and whether a doctor should override an AI diagnosis. No speaker's conclusion is established.
Chips and models. SK Hynix will advance up to 50 percent of initial development costs to its vendors and will pay suppliers for completed work even if a project misses its targets. Trinity Fab is scheduled to open in May 2027, with a 3,305 square metre clean room for lithography, etching, deposition, and inspection on 12-inch wafers. Alibaba's Qwen 4 Max is reported to cut the average task cost from 4.43 dollars to 1.67 dollars. It is described as outperforming its predecessor, using fewer tokens, and offering lower API prices to enterprise users. No parameter count is given.
The lineup. The afternoon briefing lists seven subjects. India's IT spending could approach 17 lakh crore rupees in 2027. Electronics exports are growing beyond smartphones. Karnataka has six technology initiatives covering AI research, robotics, and semiconductors. Accenture and Google Cloud plan AI education for more than 1,000 Indian institutions. Nvidia has a new board committee for national security and export controls. Isomorphic Labs has raised 5 billion dollars for AI drug development. Nvidia reports record revenue of 115.8 billion dollars under interim chief executive Colette Kress. The 103 percent increase, the 130 billion dollar forecast, the 16.94 lakh crore figure, the non-smartphone breakdown, and Suzanne Norah Johnson are not on that list.

Wednesday 18 November 2026, retrieved at 07:02 IST. Sarvam says its 105-billion-parameter model now returns 330 tokens a second for a single user, at an introductory 10 rupees per million input tokens. Bengaluru Tech Summit registrations have crossed 10,000, with 140 knowledge sessions planned. The United States is requiring licenses for AI chip exports to five countries.
The morning's through-line: Sarvam is pricing Token Factory at 10 rupees per million input tokens and reporting 330 tokens a second on its 105-billion-parameter model, the Bengaluru Tech Summit has passed 10,000 registrations, and the United States is requiring AI chip export licenses for five countries.
Sarvam's speed. Sarvam reports a 2.86-times throughput increase on its own 105-billion-parameter model, to 330 tokens a second for a single user, after custom kernels and a three-tier cache. The introductory price is 10 rupees per million input tokens. The company says the cache hits 95.7 percent across more than 450 billion tokens a day. The headline names this Token Factory. A separate report launches Token Factory with the Sarvam 105B model for enterprise inference, and says on-premise deployment is available for organisations that need local data control. Its headline price is 10 rupees per million input tokens. Its body says input pricing starts at 10 rupees and does not repeat "per million". It calls the 95.7 percent figure a DeepSeek cache hit rate, not a prompt-cache rate, and it does not give the 330-token speed, the 2.86-times gain, or the 450 billion tokens a day.
The summit. Delegate registrations have crossed 10,000, with 140 knowledge sessions planned. An India-US tech conclave is set for 18 November. AI hackathons on physical AI, agriculture, and healthcare carry a combined prize pool of 15 lakh rupees, plus another 15 lakh rupees in AI credits. A Future Makers Conclave on 19 November brings founders and investors together around deep tech. Karnataka's IT and biotechnology minister is named as Priyanker. Further wording puts semiconductor manufacturing, hardware sovereignty, and openings for Indian component suppliers on the agenda, and says the 18 November conclave will discuss quantum collaboration, critical minerals, pack silica, and cyber security. Software Technology Parks of India is sponsoring exhibition space for around 100 startups in IT, IT-enabled services, and electronics. Hackathon winners can also receive a residency given as bhatwan.ai. The spellings Priyanker, pack silica, and bhatwan.ai are uncertain. A second report's headline puts the summit at 140 sessions and a 50,000 square foot robot pavilion. Its body says more than 10,000 registered delegates are looking at chips and edge AI, and that Karnataka has tech growth targets and Kalaburagi a rising economic contribution, with no figures for either. Venue coverage describes the 29th edition at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre as India's biggest tech event. AIM is a media partner. Antara Gupta is in the studio and Sudhi Sachdev, principal anchor, is at the venue. The scale given there is more than 10,000 delegates, more than 1,500 exhibitors, more than 700 speakers, and 65 countries. Karnataka's AI university is a plan. Also named, without conclusions, are a government AI rollout, a deep tech fund, a quantum centre, letters of intent still to be tracked, robot dogs and humanoids, Microsoft's Shiksha Copilot for teachers, healthcare, voice AI in Indian languages, assistive technology, and government sandboxes.
CtrlS. CtrlS has signed a letter of intent for a 150 MW AI facility, with a proposed investment of 10,000 crore rupees. That project is not built. Separately, the Patna data center opened in October. The company puts it at 400 crore rupees and 12 MW of IT load, with room to expand. A different report says CtrlS is scaling toward 4.4 gigawatts of capacity by 2030 and plans more than 20 new edge facilities, with Bihar as a hub after the Patna launch. That report's headline says 20 more edge centers and puts the Patna site at 400 crore rupees. No opening date is given for the next sites. The 150 MW letter, the 10,000 crore proposal, and the 12 MW load are not in that report.
Chips and models. The United States is requiring licenses for AI chip exports to five countries, to close a loophole Chinese firms have used to reach advanced hardware. The five countries are not named. Restrictions on remote data-center access are being tightened for national security. No market move is stated. India has joined the San Francisco Declaration, described as a US-led effort, alongside ten other nations. The partnership is aimed at the supply of chips, manufacturing equipment, and energy networks. Five working groups cover innovation policy, AI adoption, and supply chain security. The wording for those groups is Paxilica, and the other countries are not named. A briefing list instead says a declaration with nine partner countries. That is a different count. SK Hynix is putting 1.4 trillion won into its supply chain and a new cleanroom, and aims to cover 50 percent of costs for local suppliers over the next five years, around the Trinity Fab site in Yongin. The headline says the money will build the Trinity Fab. No budget split and no completion date are given. Alibaba has launched Qwen4-Max for enterprise workloads. The headline spells it Qwen 4 Max, puts it at 2.4 trillion parameters, and says task cost is down 62 percent. The body states a 35 percent reduction in token use and a 62 percent decrease in API task costs, and describes cybersecurity safeguards for enterprise use. The 2.4 trillion figure is not repeated in the body.
The conversations. Sudhi Sachdev speaks with Bolna founders Maitreya Wagh and Prateek Sachan about voice agents for India, from multilingual calls to banks and enterprises. Bolna went from five Y Combinator rejections and a pivot to handling millions of voice calls a day. The headline says 1.3 million-plus daily calls. The Symphony Summit is on 20 November. How the company chooses speech, language, and voice models, why Assamese and Odia still lag, and what banks require are subjects of the conversation. What the founders concluded is not established. Sthanika AI is launching in Hyderabad. Sudhi Sachdev speaks with Sridhar Muppidi, co-founder of PurpleTalk Inc., about why the Hyderabad lab built a decision model and how many agent tasks need a large language model. The headline calls it India's Sieve Decision Model. That name is not used in the body. No cost saving is given. The Bharat EduAI Stack is presented with a new Bodhan AI Centre of Excellence at IIT Madras, and with AI moving into government schools. Anoop of Bodhan AI, who spent more than eight years at Microsoft, is building sovereign open-weight models for Indian languages: Indic-Transcribe, Indic-Speak, Indic-OCR, and Indic-Translate. Nandan Nilekani's proposal is to generate NTA question papers on the day of the exam to prevent leaks. It is a proposal. Who will govern the stack, and how schools deploy it without large hardware budgets, is asked and not answered. AI tutors for classes 6 to 12, and AI as a co-pilot for teachers, are subjects, not measured results. SpaceX caught the Starship upper stage with tower arms after about 22.5 hours in flight. The headline says the catch was midair and came after 22.5 hours in orbit.
The list. The briefing names seven subjects: physical AI at the Bengaluru Tech Summit, with robotics demonstrations and startup competitions; CtrlS targeting 4.4 gigawatts by 2030; India's declaration with nine partner countries on AI supply chains; Sarvam's Token Factory; SK Hynix investing 1.4 trillion won in its chip suppliers; Alibaba's Qwen4-Max; and a US rule requiring export licences for advanced AI chips to five nations. The 150 MW letter of intent, the Patna megawatts, the 330-token rate, and the "ten other nations" wording are not on that list. Nothing beyond the list is established.

Tuesday 17 November 2026, retrieved at 07:03 IST. SpaceX caught Starship Ship 42 with tower arms after 14 orbits and 22.5 hours. Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia after 33 years, and Colette Kress is interim chief executive while the board looks for a successor. The morning's through-line: SpaceX caught Starship Ship 42 after 14 orbits and 22.5 hours, Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia with Colette Kress as interim chief, and ReNew has committed 80,000 crore rupees to Andhra Pradesh, including a 1 gigawatt green data center.
Ship 42. SpaceX recovered Starship Ship 42 with a precise mid-air catch by mechanical tower arms after the vehicle completed 14 orbits and 22.5 hours. The catch is a completed recovery and a milestone for the programme. Engineers are preparing to inspect the ship's heat shield for orbital wear. No inspection result is given. The recovery is a critical step toward rapid reusability. The upper stage was caught at Starbase.
Huang resigns. Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia after 33 years. Colette Kress has stepped in as interim chief executive while the board searches for a permanent successor. The change is described as bringing immediate scrutiny of customer relationships and of Nvidia's stability. AMD revenue jumped 45 percent to 13.4 billion dollars. No period is given for that jump. Elon Musk is raising concerns about deal risks, and the deal is not named. There are reports that Google Tensor Processing Units may move to Oracle. Nobody is quoted.
The summit. The Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026 is described as the 29th edition of Asia's largest integrated technology summit. It runs from 17 to 19 November at the Bangalore International Exhibition Centre under the theme AI and Beyond. The announced guests are D.K. Shivakumar, chief minister of Karnataka; Priyank Kharge, minister for home, information technology, biotechnology and e-governance; Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, executive chairperson of Biocon and chairperson of the state's Vision Group on Biotechnology; Pratik Gandhi, actor, storyteller and theatre practitioner; and Puneet Chandok, president of Microsoft India and South Asia. No remarks from them were available at 07:03 IST.
Adobe and Google. Adobe is adding Gemini to Acrobat and an edit option inside Google Drive. The partnership also connects Gmail and Google Drive with Adobe Acrobat, presented as a simpler way to handle documents for enterprise creative work. AI assistance can resize images through conversational commands, for people who manage social media assets. That resize feature is not identified as Gemini.
ChatGPT Wallet. OpenAI is rolling out ChatGPT Wallet so users in the United States can pay with Visa, Mastercard, or American Express. The buyer reviews the seller, the purchase, the total, and the card, then approves with Face ID or a fingerprint. The payment network issues a token for checkout, so the real card details stay hidden from the agent and the seller, and are not exposed to the assistant. Approval is biometric. Approval and a completed order are separate steps.
The lineup. ReNew Energy Global's 80,000 crore rupee investment in Andhra Pradesh is to build the state's clean energy supply chain. Karnataka's LEAP programme is to spread tech jobs beyond Bengaluru. QpiAI has inaugurated an Asia-scale Phase 2 quantum chip foundry in Bengaluru. Jio plans a 1,600-satellite constellation. ChatGPT Wallet lets agents complete purchases in the United States once the user approves. Adobe and Google are bringing their AI tools closer. Nvidia's leadership change opens a chip contest. SpaceX caught Starship's upper stage at Starbase. Nothing beyond those subjects is established.
Jio's satellites. Jio is building a constellation of 1,600 satellites to connect 6 lakh villages and to move from leasing bandwidth to owning the orbital hardware. Partnerships with ISRO, SpaceX, and Skyroot are intended to support the launch. Technical and regulatory hurdles are still open. Rocket capacity is still a constraint, spectrum allocation is still pending, and those two issues are what the plan's ability to compete is said to depend on. No launch date is given.
The foundry. QpiAI has inaugurated Phase 2 of a quantum chip foundry in India, placed in Bengaluru. The plant fabricates flip chip superconducting processors and is built around an advanced clean room described as one of the largest of its kind in Asia. QpiAI is already using it to manufacture its own processor lines. The company plans 10,000-qubit chips, and the foundry is a step toward building a 10,000-qubit quantum computer locally. Those chips are not described as already made. The foundry's work is the development of indigenous superconducting chips. The plant is also called Asia-scale.
Kalaburagi. Karnataka wants Kalaburagi, also spelled Kalaburgi, to rise from 1.9 percent to 3 percent of state GDP as technology growth moves beyond Bengaluru. The roadmap includes proposed financial support for deep-tech founders and allocating 1 crore in funding for emerging startups outside the capital. Whether that 1 crore has been released is not stated. No job target is given.
ReNew in Andhra. ReNew has committed 80,000 crore rupees to Andhra Pradesh. The money funds a 1 gigawatt green data center and advanced silicon manufacturing, aimed at the electricity demand tied to AI. The deployments are in Anakapalli and are tied to industrial scaling and workforce development there. No job count and no completion date are given. The same report looks at the semiconductor industry after recent executive leadership changes and does not name the executive or the company. Separately, ReNew is investing 11,000 crore rupees in polysilicon and metallurgical silicon plants. That spending adds to a 6.5 gigawatt ingot and wafer plant already under construction. The 11,000 crore figure is not described as a slice of the 80,000 crore commitment.

Sunday 15 November 2026, retrieved at 07:02 IST. Kaynes Semicon has a semiconductor packaging plant in Sanand, Gujarat, described as one of the OSAT facilities approved under the India Semiconductor Mission. The morning's through-line: Kaynes Semicon is packaging chips in Sanand under the India Semiconductor Mission, ZenteiQ's Dhīr is built to run offline in English and ten Indian languages, and Point Break asks whether 45,000 subsidised GPUs still leave Indian startups short of research, funding, and talent.
Kaynes in Sanand. Kaynes Semicon has a new semiconductor plant in Sanand, Gujarat, described as one of India's approved OSAT facilities under the India Semiconductor Mission. Sanjana Gupta tours the plant with Raghu Panicker, chief executive of Kaynes SemiCon. The account covers the change from barren land to a working unit, and the work inside the clean room. Chips are packaged and tested from wafer saw through final testing. The steps named are wafer mount, die attach, wire bonding, moulding, and testing. The special economic zone is described as speeding up customs clearance. The plant cleared around 35 licenses in eight months. Reliability and failure analysis are described as keeping chip quality near 100 percent. Panicker is not quoted. No production volume and no opening date are given.
Dhīr offline. Dhīr is a small open-source language model from ZenteiQ that the account says runs entirely offline. The example is a phone in aeroplane mode asked a question in Odia. Familiar systems wait for a signal, and Dhīr is presented as working without one. It is built to support English and ten Indian languages, and it aims to put sovereign AI on local servers and mobile devices. The account says India has announced sovereign AI before, and that many of those announcements are still waiting for a first customer. Whether Dhīr is a working product or another theoretical launch inside the IndiaAI Mission, given as 10,371 crore rupees, is left open. Professor Sashikumaar Ganesan of the Indian Institute of Science, founder of ZenteiQ, is the person the account sits down with to test the claims. No finding from that conversation is given.
The GPU question. Point Break host Antara Gupta asks whether a GPU shortage still explains India lagging in the global AI race. The account says hardware has been the usual excuse, and that the excuse is running out of time because the government has scaled the IndiaAI Mission to over 45,000 GPUs and is subsidising compute for startups. The title calls that 45,000 figure a myth and asks whether Indian AI startups are stuck in a subsidy trap. The question put to the guests is whether a lack of servers is being blamed for deeper problems in fundamental research, funding, and talent pipelines. The guests are Amit Sheth, chief executive of IAIRO; Vishnu Subramaniam, founder of Jarvislabs.ai; and Ramesh Pudhucode, tech advisor at Primerica. Their answers are not given.

Saturday 14 November 2026, retrieved at 07:01 IST. JPMorgan's forecast puts 400,000 humanoid robots into US manufacturing and logistics as the industry moves from demos to commercial deployment. CleanMax and Blackstone-backed Neysa plan a 2-gigawatt compute factory in Kurnool at 8,000 crore rupees. A later account says Jensen Huang has stepped down after an independent board probe. An earlier account said a removal was not a decision already taken, and another said the board still had full confidence in him.
The morning's through-line: JPMorgan sees 400,000 humanoid robots filling US factory and logistics jobs, Kurnool is the site of a planned 2-gigawatt compute factory, and a later account says Jensen Huang has stepped down after a board probe that earlier accounts do not treat as a departure.
The robot forecast. JPMorgan has released a forecast that humanoid robots are moving from viral demos to commercial deployment. The United States is preparing for 400,000 robots to fill severe labor shortages in manufacturing and logistics. Hardware costs are dropping to a level that rivals human wages. The larger change is in software. The latest AI brain models from Google DeepMind and Nvidia are described as solving the main robotic bottleneck and setting up a large factory transformation. No year is given for the 400,000 figure.
The California suit. A coalition of nonprofits has filed a lawsuit to block companies including OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Anthropic from building frontier AI models. The suit uses California public nuisance law. The plaintiffs use the executives' own apocalyptic warnings and demand a total freeze on development. The account asks whether a California judge could stop work toward artificial superintelligence. It does not report a ruling. It looks at the US industry as it contends with state-level injunctions while trying to stay ahead of China. The plaintiffs are not named.
The glasses. Google and Samsung have launched Intelligent Eyewear, starting at 395 dollars. The glasses weigh 41 grams, run on the Android XR platform, and include Hey Gemini conversational AI. They are aimed at Meta's Ray-Ban glasses. Privacy safeguards are described as a way to avoid the stigma the account calls Glasshole. Whether this walled-garden hardware wins the wearable market is left open. No on-sale date and no country are given.
The leadership account. This account says Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has stepped down after an independent board probe, and it calls the situation a political and corporate firestorm. It describes him as the person who built the hardware layer of the AI revolution. It says the investigation centers on an alleged affair with a businesswoman suspected by US intelligence of acting as a Chinese asset. She is not named. It says US lawmakers are demanding aggressive export controls and that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is facing heavy scrutiny, and it calls the situation a leadership crisis for the semiconductor industry. Huang, the board, and Lutnick are not quoted. An earlier account said shares fell more than 8 percent on reports of a possible removal, with results due on 17 November, and that a removal was not a decision already taken. A still earlier account said the board maintained full confidence in Huang while searching for successors. This account is a different claim. It does not say Nvidia has confirmed a departure.
The voice model. Chariot, founded by former Google DeepMind and Meta researchers, has launched a text-to-speech model for 11 Indian languages. The account places that launch in New Delhi. The model mixes more than one language inside a single sentence, which the account calls code-mixing, and it uses contextual reasoning to settle pronunciation. Chariot is backed by the IndiaAI Mission, given as 10,372 crore rupees. Whether the company can challenge ElevenLabs and OpenAI in the enterprise market is left open. The founders are not named.
The satellites. Bengaluru-based Astrome Technologies has secured 64.05 crore rupees from the Technology Development Board. The money is for what the account calls India's first sovereign, AI-powered electronic-intelligence satellite constellation. The 50-kilogram microsatellites are to operate in low Earth orbit, use links between satellites and AI software on the ground, and intercept and process electronic signals for persistent defense surveillance. No launch date and no number of satellites are given.
The Kurnool factory. The account calls electricity one of the biggest bottlenecks in AI. CleanMax and Blackstone-backed Neysa have partnered on a 2-gigawatt AI compute factory in Kurnool, Andhra Pradesh, at 8,000 crore rupees. The 600-acre site is scheduled for completion in March 2028. Bengaluru's deep-tech startups have raised 3.77 billion dollars since 2010, more than twice Delhi NCR at 1.64 billion dollars. The figures are attributed to the Bengaluru Innovation Report 2026, released at the Bengaluru Tech Summit on 18 November and prepared by the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission and 314 Capital. The total is cumulative since 2010, with data updated to 23 September, so it is not money raised in 2026 alone. Chennai is third, at about 1.41 billion dollars, ahead of Mumbai and Hyderabad. Hyderabad has more deep-tech companies than Chennai, while Chennai's companies have raised more. Bengaluru accounts for 36.3 percent of India's native-AI startup funding. The spoken count is 799 such startups in the city, 764 of them active and funded. The description says over 799. AI and deep tech should not be added together, because a company can be both. item.title: OpenAI's Control Room rejects the next model output within 35 seconds of a stop
item.description:

item.title: Google.org's $2.3 million screening grant, cut down to a short
item.description:
Google.org is putting 2.3 million dollars into a Pune startup so health workers can be sent to high-risk neighborhoods instead of screening everyone. The short gives the grant and the method. It does not repeat the tuberculosis pilot counts from Wednesday's longer report, and its description does not print the company name.

Key points

  • The grant is 2.3 million dollars from Google.org, plus 200,000 dollars in Google Cloud credits and technical support, to expand an AI disease-screening platform.
  • The description says the app is offline, in local languages, and built for frontline health workers. It tells them where to go. It uses government health data and Google's Earth AI models to flag high-risk zones of about 300 metres.
  • The spoken extract adds local factors: settlement density, rainfall and flooding. It then says the app plans household visits. The auto-caption's last noun is "roots," which is not a clean word.
  • The description calls it "a Pune startup" and does not name it. The auto-caption renders a name close to "Franc.ai" and an app close to "MAI Netra." Wednesday's report spelled the company Froncort.AI on the lower third and the app mAI-Netra, and the automatic caption of that report garbled the company name. This short does not show the spelling.
  • Wednesday's report also gave the Maharashtra tuberculosis comparison, the cost figures, and the caveat that the tool has not been shown to find more patients. Those numbers are not in this short.

The card reads "Google Backs an AI That Finds the Uncounted Sick." item.description:

Key points

  • The narration opens with exporters having a tariff problem as well. Indian auto parts face duty of up to about 25 percent in the United States.
  • A trade framework in February promised relief. It is still not final. A burned-in caption reads "in February promised."
  • The commerce minister said the EU should offer zero duty by March or April. The description calls him the commerce minister. The burned-in caption spells the name Goyal, in the line "Goyal also said the EU." The auto-caption says "Mr. Goyel." Wednesday's export report named Piyush Goyal.

item.title: Gemini Robotics 2.5 hits 96 percent on a Mercedes kitting pilot
item.description:
Google DeepMind says Gemini Robotics 2.5, announced on 10 November, got a humanoid through a Mercedes-Benz kitting job at 96 percent. This is a Front Page report. The caption track runs to 2 minutes 55 seconds. The anchor's caveat is that a factory pilot is not a fully automated line, and that Google's lab numbers are not a guarantee for every robot or workplace.

Key points

  • Gemini Robotics 2.5 is a vision-language-action model. The narration says it turns what a robot sees, and what it is told, into physical movement.
  • Google evaluated it on more than 200 tasks, including delicate objects, tool use, and sorting components. The company says success rates rose 30 to 100 percent over previous baselines, depending on the task, and completion times fell 20 to 30 percent. The anchor says those are Google's evaluation results, not a guarantee for every robot or workplace.
  • The factory test used Apollo 2 humanoid robots at Mercedes-Benz production sites in Germany and Hungary. The job was automotive kitting: pick metal brackets out of bulk bins and place them in trays in the sequence the line needs. Google reports a 96 percent success rate for that proof of concept.
  • Two models split the work. Gemini Robotics 2.5 controls the hands and arms. A separate Gemini Robotics embodied-reasoning model manages the workflow.
  • On safety, Google says new guidance raised safe task completion by 33 percent around obstacles and by 43 percent around nearby people, in its own evaluations.
  • The model is rolling out to Google's robotics partners. It is not being released as a general consumer product.
  • DeepMind's 10 November post, which this report is summarizing, names the robot maker as Apptronik and the lines as Kecskemét in Hungary and Sindelfingen in Germany. The narration names Apollo 2, Germany, and Hungary, and does not name the company or the cities. The same post does not say how many picks the 96 percent covers, how long the pilot ran, or how the cycle time compared with a person. The AIM report does not say that either.
  • The Front Page take: the breakthrough is a robot that can repeat a task safely, accurately, and economically thousands of times. This is a meaningful step. A successful pilot is not the same as a fully automated production line.

From the video

The caption track was retrieved and runs to 2 minutes 55 seconds. hq2.jpg is a broadcast frame: a woman anchor at a laptop, with a humanoid beside blue bins and a Mercedes-Benz sign, under the lines "GOOGLE UNVEILS GEMINI ROBOTICS 2.5" and "96% SUCCESS IN FACTORY PILOT." hq3.jpg is the same anchor alone, under "THE FRONT PAGE TAKE." She is not named on screen or in the narration. maxresdefault.jpg is the poster the channel marks as made with AI assistance. It shows a bald man with glasses beside a humanoid, with DeepMind and Google marks. That portrait is not named, and the poster is not treated as footage. The full video file could not be downloaded after a bot check, so the frames and the caption track are the video record used here.

item.title: Meta lists Muse at 1,799 and 8,999 rupees in India before the launch
item.description:
Meta has India prices up for its personal AI agent Muse even though Indian users cannot officially use it yet. The report, just under three minutes, says the useful test is not whether Muse can plan a trip. It is whether Muse can complete the booking, safely, and with permission. The prices come from The Hindu's reading of Meta's subscription page, and Meta has not confirmed them.

Key points

  • The narration says Indian users cannot officially access Muse as of this report. A lower third says the India launch date is still unknown. Users are still being placed on a wait list.
  • According to The Hindu, Meta's Muse subscription page lists 1,799 rupees for the power tier and 8,999 rupees for the maximum tier. The anchor calls the top tier nearly 9,000 rupees.
  • Subscriptions billed through Google Play or Apple may cost slightly more. Meta has not confirmed that the prices are final, and the billing period for the India amounts has not been specified. Meta did not respond to the newspaper's queries.
  • Muse launched in September. It is built to take action, not only to answer questions: sending and managing email, planning travel, filling forms, and making bookings. People can use the Muse app or WhatsApp.
  • Meta says Muse runs on a dedicated cloud computer, with controls so a user can review and approve important actions.
  • The Hindu reports that Muse crossed 10 million downloads in its first two months.
  • The agent cannot currently get authorization to make card payments for Indian users, because the payment-processor integrations are not available there. The narration says charging premium prices before local access and payments are in place could be difficult, and that WhatsApp is Meta's distribution advantage in India. India, it says, needs an agent that can get things done.

From the video

hq2.jpg shows a male anchor in a white shirt and glasses at the desk. The lower third reads "META MUSE PRICES SURFACE IN INDIA" and "INDIA LAUNCH DATE STILL UNKNOWN." hq3.jpg is the same anchor alone, with no lower third. item.title: Andhra Pradesh clears a 512 MW AI data center, and the job math splits from the Google claim
item.description:
On Tuesday the Andhra Pradesh cabinet approved a 512-megawatt AI data center costing 31,387 crore rupees. Reports put the jobs at about 1,000. The state's IT minister has said Google's 1-gigawatt hub in Visakhapatnam would create at least two lakh jobs. The report sets those claims side by side, then looks at water, power and the factory projects cleared in the same sitting. This is a five-minute Front Page report.

Key points

  • The cabinet cleared a 512-megawatt AI data center at 31,387 crore rupees. Reports put employment at about 1,000, which the narration works out to about two jobs a megawatt.
  • In April the state's IT minister said Google's 1-gigawatt hub in the same city would create at least two lakh jobs. The narration also quotes a running figure of 188,000 to 200,000 direct and indirect jobs once the hub is operating, about 200 jobs a megawatt. Both numbers come from the same state.
  • Experts quoted by The Federal put the Google jobs figure at 20,000 to 30,000. The cabinet's own number for a data center about half that size sits much closer to the experts than to two lakh.
  • The same meeting approved a robotics and physical AI policy through 2036, a gaming and animation policy through 2031, and changes to the semiconductor fab policy. The reports the desk found did not include the incentives or the targets, so the narration calls the policies promises for now.
  • Two factory approvals are the jobs comparison. One is 570 crore rupees and 2,565 jobs at Rambilli. Ravali Spinners is 237 crore rupees and 1,569 jobs in the Godavari region. That is about 22 lakh and 15 lakh rupees of investment per job. Together, about 807 crore rupees and 4,134 jobs. The data center is about 39 times the investment for under a quarter of the jobs.
  • Land does not always become a factory. At Naidupeta, where a 4,000-crore advanced-materials plant was cleared, the cabinet took back land it had earlier given to Websol Renewables and Metro Decorative.
  • The state wants 6.5 gigawatts of data centers around Visakhapatnam. About six ventures were named, including Google and Reliance. Reliance received 25 acres at Bhogapuram on Tuesday.
  • The city gets about 410 million litres of water a day against a demand of 480 million litres. The minister says data-center water will come from Polavaram through dedicated pipelines and that drinking water will not be touched. A former IAS officer, whose name the caption did not render cleanly, wants an independent water audit.
  • On power, the cabinet approved biogas plants, a study of small nuclear reactors, and a 15-megawatt waste-to-energy plant. The narration calls those sensible and small beside a 512-megawatt data center.
  • The Front Page take: the state has moved faster than most on land and policy, and a bet this size needs honest numbers. Before the next project is cleared, publish the jobs, the power and the water for every project already approved.

From the video

A sampled frame shows the anchor at the desk and a lower third reading "AP approves 31,387 cr data center" and "State targets 6.5 GW data center capacity," beside coastal footage with a Google mark. The published poster is a separate image. The channel says its thumbnails are made with AI assistance and are representational: this one places a portrait in front of a rendered Visakhapatnam data-center building labeled 31,387 crore and 512 MW. The portrait is not named on the poster.

  • The video title says the key protections were proved in four weeks.

item.title: Google.org puts $2.3 million into Froncort.AI to aim TB screening
item.description:
Google.org is backing the Pune startup Froncort.AI with 2.3 million dollars so health workers can be sent to the neighborhoods where tuberculosis is more likely, instead of screening everyone. The report's own caveat is that the pilot has not shown the tool finds more patients. This is a four-minute Front Page report. The company name is Froncort.AI on the lower third. The automatic caption garbles it.

Key points

  • The grant is 2.3 million dollars from Google.org, plus 200,000 dollars in Google Cloud credits and technical support, to expand an AI disease-screening platform.
  • The app is mAI-Netra. It is offline, in local languages, and built for frontline health workers. It tells them where to go rather than screening everyone.
  • It combines government health data with Google's Earth AI models and local factors, including settlement density, rainfall and flooding, and flags high-risk zones of about 300 metres. It then plans household visits and routes.
  • Tuberculosis comes first. Six diseases are planned, including malaria, dengue and cholera. The stated reach is up to eight districts in three states, potentially two to three million people.
  • In a pilot with the Maharashtra state TB programme, AI-guided teams screened 66,095 people and found 10 lab-confirmed cases. A standard campaign screened 177,322 people and found 9. The anchor's ratios are about 6,610 people screened per lab-confirmed case, against about 19,700.
  • Froncort says the cost per confirmed case fell from about 27.6 lakh rupees to 9.3 lakh rupees, and 92 percent of frontline workers reported a lighter workload.
  • The catch, stated in the report: the two campaigns were not run at the same time, the standard campaign had a mobile chest X-ray van and the AI team did not, and the numbers are small. Counting every confirmed case, not only those verified by the same lab test, the AI arm found 15 against 32.
  • The conclusion on air: AI may help target screening more efficiently, and it has not yet been shown to find more patients. A larger simultaneous trial is what the anchor says is needed.
  • Froncort is one of 15 organizations in Google.org's 30 million dollar AI for government innovation challenge. Unlike tools that read chest X-rays, this one decides where to screen.

From the video

One frame shows the anchor beside street footage of a small team walking, under the lines "Google.org backs Froncort.AI with $2.3M" and "Offline app built for frontline workers." A later frame is the anchor alone on "The Front Page take." The poster, which the channel marks as AI-assisted, shows a community health worker, a phone labeled mAI-NETRA, and a map of TB risk zones with cholera, dengue and malaria listed beside tuberculosis.

item.title: Anthropic ships Claude sheets, whiteboards and data, and asks what is left of the workbook
item.description:
Anthropic has added Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards and Claude Data. The report's point is not that Excel died overnight. It is that a team can now start the work inside Claude and only later open the specialist app. This is a four-minute Front Page report. The anchor says Excel survived the night, and then asks why a person opens it in the first place.

Key points

  • The three tools named as shipped are Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards and Claude Data. Claude Meetings is described as coming soon. The idea there is that Claude joins a call, takes notes, and updates the documents the team is already working on.
  • The product example: a team sketches a launch on a whiteboard. Claude turns the plan into a spreadsheet with owners, deadlines and a budget. When the numbers arrive, Claude Data can pull from sources such as Snowflake or Salesforce and help turn them into a dashboard.
  • People can edit the sheet together, change formulas and move between tabs. Claude is supposed to carry the context from the original plan so nobody restates the whole project.
  • Anthropic calls the wider move interactive connectors. Partners including Adobe and Atlassian can embed parts of their apps inside Claude. The records can stay in Atlassian while more of the work starts in Claude. The software still does the job. It may no longer be the first tab opened.
  • For Microsoft, the test the anchor names is how often people reach for Claude to make a tracker or pull together a report. For a startup that sells one workflow as its whole product, the question is what a customer will still pay extra for if Claude does the basic version.
  • Anthropic's own example is its legal team. They built a Slack tool that flags edits against the team's legal playbook before a lawyer reviews the draft. The company says broad marketing reviews fell from three days to about 24 hours.
  • The Front Page take: Microsoft can keep the workbook and Atlassian can keep the project record. Claude wants to be the place where a plan becomes something the team can run. Someone still has to spot the case where Claude's budget adds up and leaves out the largest expense.

From the video

A sampled frame shows the anchor at the desk and a lower third reading "Anthropic launches new workplace tools" and "Teams can co-edit AI-generated spreadsheets," with b-roll of people working on laptops at a shared table. The poster is a separate AI-assisted thumbnail of a sample Claude whiteboard, a pie-launch timeline with a prompt asking Claude to map the plan.

item.title: Sandeep Shukla on AI agents that reached live Indian systems with plain-text keys
item.description:
Sudhi Sachdev interviews Sandeep Shukla, director of IIIT Hyderabad, on a CERT-In report that AI agents reached live Indian systems using passwords and keys left in plain text. The morning shorts on fundamentals, fresher hiring and threat models are clips of this conversation. The caption track for the full interview was blocked, so the chapter list below is the video's published table of contents, not a summary of each answer. The chapters run to 58:33.

Key points

  • The title and the description state the news peg: CERT-In reported that AI agents reached live Indian systems using passwords and keys left in plain text. Shukla is there to explain the agent risk, prompt injection, phishing and the post-quantum threat.
  • The lower third on the preview frames says "Agents in live systems, nobody noticed" and "AI exploits plain text secrecy keys."
  • The description says his centre signed an agreement with NPCI on 24 October.
  • Published chapters, in order: the CERT-In advisory and cyber hygiene, the DPDP Act and data risk, AI agents versus careless humans, bug-bounty culture in India, attackers and defenders using AI, prompt injection and defences, honey tokens and decoy credentials, threat modeling with AI, AI phishing and how to spot it, the NPCI partnership and UPI fraud, the human in the loop, who trains junior talent, India's quantum mission, and a final message.
  • What he says inside those chapters is not repeated here, because the spoken track could not be retrieved. Two of the arguments are already in this morning's shorts, in his own words: students still need the fundamentals to criticize what a model writes, and a person still has to throw out a threat-model scenario the model invented.

From the video

The preview frames are a split screen. Sudhi Sachdev, labeled AIM, is on the left in a navy polo. Sandeep Shukla is on the right, labeled Director, IIIT Hyderabad. The lower third carries the plain-text-keys line. The poster is a separate AI-assisted graphic with a CERT-In sign, an "unauthorised access" panel and a quantum-security prop. item.title: Point Break asks if degrees still hold once AI enters the classroom
item.description:
Antara Gupta hosts a 50-minute Point Break debate with Vishwas Deoskar, CEO of the Indian Institute of Creative Technologies, and Prashant Pandit, CEO of Eros Wellness and co-CEO of Eros AIvidya. The question is whether universities are preparing students for an AI-first economy or printing degrees. Three of this morning's shorts are cuts of this conversation: the film-school point, the teacher-retraining point, and the tier-2 cities point.

Key points

  • The host opens with a NITI Aayog figure: 91 percent of graduates end up in jobs unrelated to what they studied. Later she cites the same gap as only about 8.25 percent of graduates working in roles aligned with their qualification. Deoskar says the 8.25 percent figure is old news, not a new AI effect.
  • Deoskar says the CBSE curriculum was built for an earlier IT and engineering demand. He works with NCERT, CBSE and IICT, and he says he has not read the AI curriculum in enough detail to confirm that AI has been laid on top of class 3. His line on teachers is that they have no choice but to retrain, because the classroom lecture is already on the student's phone. The foundation still matters. His example, which is also a short, is that smartphones retired the analog phone and the camera phone retired the film camera.
  • Pandit says Eros is in talks with the Maharashtra SSC board. He puts that board at 1.4 crore students in classes 9 to 12. He is not trying to start at class 3. The chairman, whom he describes as an IAS officer, wants AI taught where students already use phones. The obstacles he names are schools without reliable internet and teachers who are not equipped.
  • His school model has three steps. Train the teachers first. A 9th-standard course is four weeks, 10th is eight, then 16 and 32 weeks as the student moves up. Hand the schools a syllabus Eros says it will refresh every six months. Ship the Eros Universe app in the first week of December, where students make things from characters, songs and dialogue in a library he puts at 12,000 films.
  • On why Eros entered education at all, Pandit repeats the point in this morning's film short. Directing, editing and cinematography cannot be taught from theory alone. The institute produces six to seven movies a year and teaches on those live projects.
  • He says NSDC, which he describes as having a one-lakh-crore annual budget aimed at trades such as plumbing and electrical work, has now accredited 37 six-month creative-media certificates, including editor, cinematographer and sound engineer. Teachers include industry veterans, and students get time on shoots and on the app. Miranda House, which he says has ranked number one in NIRF for six years, will launch 15 creative-media courses with Eros from 1 January, and has made an exception so the courses are open to men and women. Each batch is also promised seven days abroad, with student exchanges at degree level.
  • Degree and master's courses he lists: creative media with AI, OTT film and digital cinema, VFX animation and gaming, entertainment and media, and fashion design. Five degrees, with a four-year master's plus honors. Talks are with Malla Reddy in Hyderabad, DY Patil in Pune, and others including Miranda House. Eight semesters, and the last semester is a full internship. He says Eros chairman Kishore Lulla sat on the UCLA board for 17 years and that the gap he saw is what these courses are meant to close. Eros is also discussing one AI subject inside medicine, dentistry, nursing and pharmacy with Malla Reddy University. Pandit says he has spoken with 10 to 15 leading Indian universities and three or four abroad, and that they were receptive.
  • Deoskar on the degree system: more than 3.75 lakh engineers graduate, and they do not all land in IT or manufacturing. He treats a change of track as normal, and he says the parental question is still "is my child a graduate?" IICT was set up by the Union Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, the Maharashtra government, CII and FICCI to feed the creative industry. He puts the global media and entertainment industry at 3.3 trillion dollars and India's revenue share at 2.3 percent. IICT has applied for UGC status as a distinct university. He says only six of those exist. It is also seeking INI status, which needs Parliament. He calls the faculty trainers, not teachers. He says this is his third university, after raising MIT in Pune and others. Practical work is 70 percent and theory 30 percent, judged as a portfolio plus a viva, because parents still want a number. He says IICT is priced at about a third of comparable outside rates because of the government backing, and that its Dolby Atmos theatre is being used for CBFC previews.
  • The host cites a Deloitte India finding that 86 percent of surveyed organizations said AI or agentic AI is transforming recruitment, and 72 percent use AI to screen resumes. She also says she believes IIT Pune has made AI allowed by default in coursework. That last point is her statement, not a figure either guest confirmed.
  • On exams, Pandit says paper leaks, including NEET, are the problem he is trying to design around, in talks with two state boards. One textbook, chapter-by-chapter mark weights, and his system generates ten papers. A four-teacher board reviews them in his office under CCTV, without phones. At 9:00 the board names which of the ten papers is used for an 11:00 exam. It is encrypted and sent to centers that print it, so the paper exists at the center for about half an hour. Answer sheets are scanned back by 17:00 the same day to a center in Chennai, checked by AI against the board's parameters, and mark sheets are promised in seven days. He wants the first pilot on two subjects, marked both by hand and by the system. He says tests already run with IIT Madras engineers were 99.9 percent successful, and he hopes that leaves a leakage window of about 0 to 1 percent. He says they have approached NEET and expects that conversation next year rather than this year.
  • On tier-2 and tier-3 students, Pandit cites an unnamed online platform with a turnover of almost 2,300 crore rupees, 60 percent of it IIT and IIM certificate or degree courses, bought mostly by students who missed the entrance or the campus. He also cites edX at 8 million students last year. He thinks cheap internet and near-universal smartphones close the gap in four to five years if online keeps growing, and he also says the change will be visible in the next two to three years. Deoskar says he has been to Bastar, that more than 70 crore smartphones are in regular use, and that Jio is pushing rates down further. IICT already runs hybrid courses with a contact programme. His warning is that a film made in Bastar and put on YouTube for 500 rupees is not the goal. Treat AI as a tool the student learns to use. A doctor is still needed, and the basics of engineering stay. Revamp the curriculum. Do not throw it out. He says IIT took about 50 years to produce more than 500 CEOs worldwide, and that Japan and South Korea started the anime and manga pipeline about 30 years ago.
  • Asked what they would change first if the system were rebuilt, Pandit says the syllabus, the curriculum and the management habit of treating AI as a competitor. A better prompt, he says, is the next step after search, and computers were not a threat in the 1980s either. Deoskar says the system has to stay inclusive: add AI to medicine and engineering, and do not block people who were never given the equipment or the research exposure.

From the video

Sampled frames are a three-shot. Lower thirds name Prashant Pandit, host Antara Gupta, and Vishwas Deoskar. The banner reads "Are Indian schools preparing for AI?" and "CBSE introduces AI curriculum for schools." The poster is a separate AI-assisted image headlined "Is AI making degrees useless?" with an 8.25 percent qualification-aligned-jobs graphic, the figure the host cites, plus the Eros AIvidya and IICT marks.

item.title: Morning Front Page live on Microsoft, Oracle, and the stories cut into today's shorts
item.description:
The morning Front Page live ran 1 hour 37 minutes from 10:22 IST, under a Microsoft and Oracle headline. Several of the morning shorts are the clipped versions of stories on this broadcast. The spoken script of the live itself could not be retrieved, so the list below is the broadcast's published rundown, and the picture of what was on screen comes from preview frames.

Key points

  • The lead line in the description: Microsoft is winding down its agreement to rent AI computing capacity from Oracle, and it is tightening oversight of neocloud infrastructure projects. No size, date or remaining-capacity figure was available beyond that sentence.
  • The rest of the published list: Salesforce positioning Slack as a work platform for Indian businesses, Hexaware's five-year AI contract with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, India's 11th place in the Ayre Index of youth AI readiness, Coforge joining SpaceX's AI partner network to deploy Grok, LTM and ServiceNow expanding AI agent deployments, Anthropic's launch of Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, and SemiAnalysis's estimate of SpaceX's data-centre buildout.
  • Slack, the youth-readiness numbers, Coforge and Grok, the Fermat and Fable proof work, and the Starbase build are already summarized from this morning's shorts. The Hexaware contract, the LTM and ServiceNow expansion, the Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 product launch, and the Microsoft and Oracle pullback are in the live's list and were not their own shorts in this scan.
  • India's 11th place on the Ayre Index is in this live's description. The morning short on the same study gives the 30.4 percent and 85.8 percent figures and does not state the rank.

From the video

The poster is an AI-assisted graphic of a hand throwing a switch from on to off between Microsoft and Oracle server racks, with a portrait of Satya Nadella. The preview frames of the broadcast are a different picture. They show Sudhi Sachdev interviewing Sandeep Shukla under the same lower third as the security interview: "Agents in live systems, nobody noticed" and "AI exploits plain text secrecy keys." That conversation was on this live.

item.title: A human has to own the AI outcome in a report for the insurance regulator
item.description:
Sandeep Shukla says a report for the insurance regulator, finalized on Tuesday and due out soon, requires someone to own what an AI system produces. The application has to be tiered, tested, and checked after it generates a decision or a document. He says the buck stops at a human. This is a short of about 84 seconds, from the same conversation as this morning's clips.

Key points

  • He says the report for the insurance regulator was finalized yesterday, relative to this short, and will be released soon. It is an AI governance framework.
  • One part of it is tiering. Figure out which tier an AI application sits in, and govern it accordingly.
  • Someone has to own the AI's outcomes. He rejects the answer that the AI created it and nobody knows how it happened.
  • Ownership means thorough testing, and a thorough check after the system generates a decision, a piece of content, or an artifact, to see that it makes sense. The owner also carries the risk of mistakes.
  • He says he is pretty sure the RBI has said the same thing, and that anyone writing an AI governance framework would say it too. The buck stops at a human, not a machine.

From the video

Shukla is on a video call, named on the lower third as director of IIIT Hyderabad. Under him, a hand holds a tablet showing an "AI Verification Audit" graphic: 1,248 total checks, 98.6 percent passed, and a failed "Opportunity Gap" row circled in red. A caption fragment reads "investigation." Those audit numbers are on the graphic. He does not speak them in this short.

item.title: Teachers have to retrain when the old tools leave the classroom
item.description:
Vishwas Deoskar's example, cut from this morning's Point Break debate, is that a new tool retires the old one, so teachers have to upgrade with it. The short is 48 seconds. He is not named on this frame. The words match his answer in the full debate.

Key points

  • When smartphones arrived, analog phones went out. When phones carried three cameras, the film camera went out.
  • Something has to leave because it no longer fits the technology in use.
  • If people have to upgrade, teachers have to upgrade too. In the full debate he ties this to class 3, 4 and 5, and he says he has not himself read the CBSE AI curriculum in detail.

From the video

The frame is a wooden table with a film camera, its back open, a roll of 35mm film marked 200, and a phone face-down so the triple-camera array is visible. The on-screen caption is the single word "cameras."

item.title: Online courses can bring tier-2 and tier-3 cities level with the metros
item.description:
Prashant Pandit says online education will close the gap between tier-2 and tier-3 cities and Mumbai and Delhi. He will not name the company in his example. The short is about 95 seconds and is a cut of his answer in the Point Break debate. He is not named on this frame. The words match.

Key points

  • He recently met a company he does not name. Its turnover is almost 2,300 crore rupees, entirely from online courses.
  • About 60 percent of what it sells are IIT and IIM courses, certificates or degrees.
  • Most of its students are from tier-2 and tier-3 cities, people who never had access to those campuses or who missed the entrance.
  • He thinks the shift shows up in four to five years if online keeps growing at this pace, and he also says it will be visible in the next two to three years. Both timeframes are in the short.
  • His reasons: India's internet rates are the cheapest in the world, and a smartphone is with almost everybody. The practical-exposure gap is what he thinks online can narrow, until those cities sit level with Mumbai and Delhi.

From the video

A young man studies at a laptop in a bedroom, a handwritten notebook and a pen on the desk, a map on the wall. The screen is a linear-algebra lesson on eigenvalues. The caption fragment reads "Somebody who don't," from the line about students who do not have that campus exposure.

item.title: Film courses need live projects, with 6 to 7 movies made each year
item.description:
A guest argues that creative-media degrees fail when they stay in the classroom. Directing, editing and cinematography need theory and practice together, so the speaker's institute produces six to seven films a year and teaches students on those live projects.

Key points

  • The guest says there is still no formal path, theoretical and practical at once, for people who want to be directors, editors or cinematographers.
  • Pure theory does not work in these courses. Editing, the guest says, cannot be taught only in a classroom. Students need practical exposure.
  • That is why the institute went into education: every year it produces six to seven movies and uses those productions as the teaching material.
  • Students are meant to leave with theoretical knowledge and a practical angle from real projects.

From the video frame

The published frame is a classroom. A young man sits at a wooden desk with a notebook and a laptop, in front of a chalkboard laid out as a film-studies lesson: a film triangle linking text, creator and audience, modes of address, narrative structure, and montage. A caption on screen reads "editor in the classroom," which is the line the guest is saying. A small logo sits in the corner. The guest is not named on this frame.

item.title: Students who skip the fundamentals cannot check what AI writes
item.description:
Sandeep Shukla, Director of IIIT Hyderabad, says students who hand programming assignments to Claude Code are taking a shortcut that backfires. Fundamentals are what let a person use AI and criticize its output. He also says he has heard that many large multinational companies are not hiring freshers this year, and he calls that decision short-sighted.

Key points

  • Students are using Claude Code and similar tools to do programming assignments. Shukla says that shortcut is a mistake.
  • The fear underneath the shortcut, as he describes it, is that nobody will hire them for programming anymore. He says that is not the case.
  • You need the fundamentals to use AI at all. You cannot trust the model blindly. Someone has to be able to check the output and criticize it, and that takes knowledge the student still has to hold.
  • On hiring, he says he has heard that a large number of MNCs are not hiring freshers this year. He calls the move short-sighted. The published description reports it the same way: many MNCs are reportedly not hiring freshers. Treat it as his account of what he has heard, not as a hiring census.

From the video frame

Split screen. On top, Sandeep Shukla on a video call, with a lower third reading "SANDEEP SHUKLA" and "DIRECTOR, IIIT HYDERABAD." Below, the anchor in a navy polo, laptop open, city-and-server-room backdrop. A caption word "and" sits between them. The clip is a conversation, not a solo anchor read.

item.title: AI can build threat models faster than humans, with a human to check
item.description:
The same guest, Sandeep Shukla, says threat models can now be drafted by AI much faster than by people, provided the model is given enough information. A human still has to reject scenarios the model invented. He anchors the point in the post-9/11 exercise that asked Hollywood producers to imagine attacks nobody in security had listed.

Key points

  • Before 9/11, passenger planes used as weapons were not in anyone's threat model: not air traffic control, not the military, and there was no Department of Homeland Security yet.
  • After the attacks, Homeland Security brought in Hollywood producers to do a threat-modeling exercise, because the missing ingredient was extreme imagination. That scenario is now a standard threat model, and the airport controls people see today come from it.
  • Known models already drive routine defenses. Ransomware is the example: backups, and isolating those backups.
  • The failures are the models nobody wrote down. His example is an attacker reading source code to find a hidden API key. It was not in the threat model, so it was not defended.
  • Given enough information, AI can produce these models faster than humans. A person still has to check that the team is not chasing a hallucinated scenario that cannot actually happen.

From the video frame

Shukla is on the upper half again, same lower third, Director, IIIT Hyderabad, mid-gesture. The lower half cuts to an airport security lane: travelers loading bags onto a belt, officers beside a scanner marked Rapiscan 620DV. The on-screen caption reads "All the controls we," matching the line about airport controls that came out of that threat model.

item.title: SpaceX went from cleared land to steel at Starbase in one month, images show
item.description:
Satellite images are used from Starbase, Texas, where SpaceX builds and launches Starship. Land that was being cleared at the end of August had steel structures up by the end of September. SemiAnalysis estimates another site near Colossus 2 could go from an empty plot to a finished building in about four months. The clip's warning is that a finished shell is the easy photograph. The next milestone is the chips inside running around the clock.

Key points

  • Starbase, Texas, is where SpaceX builds and launches Starship.
  • Satellite images at the end of August showed land being cleared. By the end of September, steel structures were going up.
  • Near Colossus 2, SemiAnalysis estimates a separate site could go from empty plot to completed building in about four months.
  • A finished building photographs well. The milestone the narration points to is when the chips in that building can run continuously.

From the video frame

An anchor in a light blazer sits with a laptop in the server-room set. Above her, the frame shows an aerial site image with the SemiAnalysis credit on screen. The graphic is the satellite view the script is walking through.

item.title: Fable agents made a Fermat proof machine-checkable in 30 hours, not 11 days
item.description:
The report corrects a circulating claim about Fermat's Last Theorem. Andrew Wiles proved it in the 1990s. What a thousand Fable agents did was rewrite that proof so a computer could check it step by step. Anthropic's earlier run of the same kind of work took 11 days. This one took 30 hours. The question the clip leaves for software teams is whether that speed makes it cheaper to verify that a program does what it is supposed to do.

Key points

  • People have been saying Claude solved Fermat's Last Theorem. The short says that is the wrong reading. Wiles proved the theorem in the 1990s.
  • A thousand Fable agents put the existing proof into a form a computer can check line by line.
  • An earlier Anthropic effort on this took 11 days. The new run took 30 hours.
  • The useful question is not the theorem. It is whether the same agent workflow lowers the cost of proving that software behaves as specified.

From the video frame

The same anchor, white blazer and laptop, with a full-screen graphic of equations behind the line she is reading. A caption fragment, "That kind of work," matches the turn from the theorem to software verification.

item.title: Coforge will deploy Grok through Momentum Blue, its human and AI agent unit
item.description:
Coforge has said how it will actually roll Grok out inside companies. Every enterprise deployment goes through Momentum Blue, the customer-facing engineering unit that embeds hybrid teams of human engineers and AI agents in the client and ties their output to agreed business targets. The technical bridge is Coforge's Neuron enterprise AI platform. Money terms were not disclosed.

Key points

  • Financial details of the partnership were not disclosed. The operating model was.
  • All Grok enterprise deployments are handled exclusively through Momentum Blue.
  • Momentum Blue is built to go past traditional IT sourcing. It places mixed teams of engineers and autonomous agents inside client organizations.
  • Those teams are explicitly tied to agreed business targets, not to a staffing contract.
  • Delivery leans on Coforge's existing AI-led modernization work, and specifically on the Neuron platform, which is supposed to connect Grok to legacy corporate software.
  • Anup Nair, chief AI commercial officer, is quoted on screen and in the narration. The audible portion: "From software modernization and customer service to enterprise applications, we bring the industry context, engineering expertise, and adoption capabilities to turn Grok's technology into solutions." The captured narration cuts off as the sentence continues.

From the video frame

Top half is a headshot of a man in a purple sweater, with a caption reading "AI Commercial Officer at," which is the role the narration assigns to Anup Nair. Bottom half is the anchor at the laptop, delivering the quote. The frame is a quote card, not a live two-shot.

item.title: 30.4 percent of young Indians are not in work, education or training, a study finds
item.description:
A youth AI-readiness study, as reported here, finds that turning readiness into jobs is the stuck part. About 30.4 percent of young Indians are not in employment, education or training, and 85.8 percent of young workers are in the informal sector. The government has started programs with Intel and has pledged to train 10 million young people in AI within a year. Calvin Ayer, founder of the Ayer think tank, says AI will change work, business and how wealth is created. The anchor adds that the wealth is gated by who has access.

Key points

  • 30.4 percent of young Indians are not in employment, education or training.
  • 85.8 percent of young workers are in the informal sector.
  • The Indian government is trying to close the gap with Intel-linked programs and a pledge to train 10 million young people in AI inside one year.
  • Calvin Ayer, founder of the Ayer think tank: "AI is going to change how we work, how we do business, and how wealth is created."
  • The narration's addition: that wealth creation is strictly gated by access.

From the video frame

A headshot of a grey-haired man sits above the anchor. The caption on the quote line reads "change how we work," the opening of Ayer's sentence. The portrait itself is not labeled with a name on this frame, so the identification comes from the narration, not from a lower third.

item.title: Salesforce bundles Agentforce, Slack and Tableau into an SMB kit bought by card
item.description:
Salesforce is aiming at India's small and mid-size businesses, which the clip calls its highest-revenue segment in the country. The offer is a plug-and-play growth kit that bundles Agentforce, Sales, Slack and Tableau, sold on a credit card so a buyer can skip a three-to-four-month enterprise rollout. The bet is autonomous agents rather than a price fight with Zoho.

Key points

  • The battleground named in the clip is small and medium businesses. SMBs are now the highest revenue-contributing segment for Salesforce in India.
  • The SMB growth kit bundles Agentforce, Sales, Slack and Tableau into one platform.
  • A small business can buy it with a credit card, bypassing the traditional three-to-four-month enterprise implementation.
  • Salesforce is described as not trying to beat local players such as Zoho on price. The wager is the value of autonomous AI agents.
  • Hunter is presented as an agentic sales-development representative that does the initial prospect outreach.
  • An internal help agent, KC, has handled more than 5 million inbound customer conversations and resolved nearly 70 percent of queries with no human intervention.

From the video frame

A studio portrait of a man in a navy suit sits above the anchor. The caption reads "Salesforce isn't trying to," the price-comparison line. The portrait has no name on this frame, so the summary does not attach the Zoho remark to a named executive beyond what the narration itself supports.
